title: AI Has Eliminated More American Jobs in Five Months Than It Did in All of 2024 and 2025 Combined
excerpt: Challenger data shows 87,714 AI-linked job cuts in 2026 so far. The tech sector is shedding workers three times faster than any other industry. For Indian H-1B holders, the 60-day clock has never felt shorter.
body:
Artificial intelligence has eliminated more American jobs in the first five months of 2026 than it did in all of 2024 and 2025 combined. The numbers, published by outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas, are no longer a forecast. They are a body count.

US employers cited AI as the reason for 87,714 job cuts between January and May 2026. In comparison, AI accounted for 54,836 layoffs in all of 2025 and 12,742 in 2024 — a combined total of 67,578 that 2026 blew past before the end of April.

In May alone, AI replaced 38,242 jobs — the highest single-month total since tracking began. AI now accounts for nearly 40 percent of all announced job cuts in the country, up from 7 percent in January.

## The Tech Sector Is Ground Zero

The technology sector absorbed the worst of it. US tech companies announced 123,000 job cuts through May, a 66 percent increase over the same period last year and nearly three times the layoffs of the next hardest-hit sector.

The companies doing the cutting are not struggling startups. They are the most profitable firms in the world.

Meta announced it was cutting 10 percent of its global staff — roughly 8,000 roles — while simultaneously redeploying 7,000 employees into AI-focused teams. The company posted record quarterly revenue around the same time. Cisco eliminated 4,000 positions, about 5 percent of its workforce, to redirect investment toward AI and security. PayPal plans to cut nearly 20 percent of its workforce — approximately 4,760 roles — over the next two to three years to accelerate AI adoption. Uber disclosed layoffs across its People and Places division. Intuit tied its 3,000 cuts to an AI-driven restructuring. ClickUp reduced headcount by 22 percent, explicitly citing AI as the path to "100-fold" productivity gains.

Oracle is reportedly redirecting $8 to $10 billion in annual cash flow toward AI data-centre construction, funded in part by workforce reductions.

## For Indian Workers, This Is Not a Layoff Cycle. It Is a Restructuring.

The distinction matters. Previous waves of tech layoffs were driven by economic downturns — overexpansion during COVID, rising interest rates, softening ad revenue. Companies cut, waited, and rehired. The roles that disappeared in 2022 largely returned in 2023.

This time is structurally different. Companies are not cutting and waiting. They are cutting and reallocating — moving money and headcount from traditional engineering, support, and middle-management roles into AI infrastructure and AI-product teams. The jobs being eliminated and the jobs being created are often fundamentally different positions.

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the US on H-1B visas, this creates a uniquely precarious situation. An H-1B holder who loses their job has 60 days to find a new employer willing to sponsor their visa. In a market where the roles being hired for require different skills than the ones being eliminated, that window becomes a cliff.

The timing is especially fraught. Representative Chip Roy of Texas unveiled the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026 just days ago, proposing to replace the H-1B lottery with a wage-based selection process and prevent companies that have recently conducted layoffs from hiring H-1B workers. The bill would also end the use of H-1B visas as a pathway to permanent residency and eliminate the Optional Practical Training programme.

## What the Numbers Actually Mean

The Challenger report puts total US job cuts in May at over 97,000 — the highest for the month since the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Layoffs have risen for three consecutive months: 48,307 in February, 60,620 in March, 83,387 in April, and now 97,000-plus in May.

Several tech industry leaders have stated publicly that most white-collar roles relying on computers could be automated within 12 to 18 months. Whether that timeline holds or not, the trajectory is clear enough: the companies with the most resources are treating AI not as a productivity tool but as a workforce substitute.

For Indian professionals who have built careers and families in America around the promise of stable tech employment, the five months of data in the Challenger report are not abstract. They are the labour market they are living in right now.
